messages.content:
You are verifying one structured PFAS study evidence record against the
complete source evidence cited by that record.

You receive:
1. the review task and task-specific extraction objective;
2. the held-out anchor identifiers;
3. one extracted evidence record; and
4. the complete source chunks or inspected source-page text referenced by the
   record.

Judge only source support and transcription. Do not reward usefulness,
verbosity, or agreement with general background knowledge.

Assess every substantive populated source-dependent field against only its
attached field-level locators. Do not create separate assessments for locator
arrays, record IDs, or formatting metadata:
- supported: the cited evidence directly supports the field and its material
  qualifiers;
- partially_supported: the core statement is supported but a material
  qualifier, condition, denominator, or scope is missing;
- unsupported: the cited evidence does not establish the field;
- contradicted: the cited evidence directly conflicts with the field.

For quantitative_findings, value must contain an actual number, censored or
approximate number, range, or explicit ND/not-detected result. A unit-shaped
string such as "nmol/L" in value with an empty unit is a unit error even when
the source mentions that concentration scale. Do not silently reinterpret one
schema field as another. Confirm that value matches value_form; explanatory
text and uncertainty belong in qualifiers.

Classify endpoint_type from the measured basis, not the source's terminology.
Parent-compound loss alone is not destruction; phase transfer is not
degradation; inorganic fluoride release or fluorine-balance closure establishes
defluorination but not mineralization. Mineralization requires direct
carbon-fate evidence such as measured CO2/inorganic carbon or a carbon balance.
If an author calls defluorination mineralization without that evidence, retain
the author phrase only as reported_term and mark endpoint_type=mineralization
unsupported with error_type=endpoint_classification.

Comparability is an analyst-derived judgment. Do not require the source to
state the comparability conclusion verbatim. Instead, judge whether its status
and reason follow conservatively from supported cited fields for matrix, PFAS
scope, scale, conditions, endpoint, unit, and denominator.

An author_reported limitation requires direct source support. A
design_inferred limitation is supported when it follows necessarily from
cited design facts; absence from the supplied packet is not a study
limitation.

Classify errors as numeric_transcription, unit, qualifier,
endpoint_classification, source_attribution, other, or none. A record is usable
only if its source identity, matrix, treatment, endpoints, and quantitative
findings are not unsupported or contradicted in a way that would mislead
  synthesis. A usable record can still contain non-core fields that synthesis
must exclude according to their field assessments.

For metric consistency, always emit separate assessments with these exact
field-path forms when the corresponding item exists:
- `quantitative_findings[i].value`;
- `quantitative_findings[i].unit`;
- `operating_conditions[i].value`;
- `operating_conditions[i].unit`;
- `endpoints[i].endpoint_type`; and
- `comparability.status`.

Other substantive fields may be assessed individually or as a whole object,
but do not omit these required assessment types and do not emit a required
field path more than once.

Report anchor_exclusion_violation=true if the source resolves to any held-out
anchor DOI, URL, exact title, or corpus source.

Return one JSON object that follows the supplied verification schema exactly.

field_assessments.reason: The record DOI/URL exactly matches the DOI provided in the source metadata (10.1021/acsestwater.5c00641; https://doi.org/10.1021/acsestwater.5c00641).

The source describes adsorption experiments using ball-milled colloidal activated carbon (CAC BM) (S07-E04) and discusses competitive adsorption behavior and mechanisms for PFAS on CAC BM (S07-E02, S07-E05). It is reasonable and accurate to state that CAC BM was the adsorbent used for the competitive adsorption experiments and that it is the same material as in the single-solute tests.

The competitive adsorption section states that bisolute experiments were conducted to evaluate how background PFAS mixtures influence competitive adsorption behavior and refers to single and binary solute systems (S07-E02). Combined with the batch adsorption experiment description using prepared PFAS solutions in flasks (S07-E03, S07-E04), this supports that the matrix is laboratory-prepared (synthetic) binary PFAS aqueous solutions used in batch adsorption tests.

The work is clearly described as laboratory batch adsorption tests using Erlenmeyer flasks with defined solution volumes and shaking (bench-scale) and includes bisolute (binary) experiments (S07-E02, S07-E03, S07-E04). Describing the scale as bench-scale batch competitive adsorption tests in binary PFAS synthetic aqueous solutions is consistent with these details.
The article reports original laboratory adsorption experiments (methods and results sections; e.g., S07-E03, S07-E05), which is consistent with classification as a primary experiment.

The competitive adsorption text reports PFBA when copresent with PFOA, PFOS, and PFBS, including their specific percentage reductions (S07-E05). This supports the description of binary combinations of PFBA with PFOA, PFOS, and PFBS.

The source states that PFOS significantly reduced the removal efficiencies of both PFBA and PFBS, giving the PFBS reduction as −30.2% (S07-E05). This implies a PFBS–PFOS binary combination, supporting the field value.

The endpoint is described in the source as the change in removal efficiency (%) between single- and binary-solute systems, with negative values indicating reduction in removal efficiency in the presence of cocontaminants (S07-E02). Classifying this as a removal-type endpoint is consistent with the measurement basis (removal efficiency).

S07-E02 explicitly states that Figure 5c illustrates the change in removal efficiency (%) between single- and binary-solute systems and that negative values indicate a reduction in removal efficiency in the presence of cocontaminants, suggesting competitive interactions. This directly supports the interpretation provided in the record.

This endpoint summarizes qualitative competitive adsorption behavior (hierarchy of PFAS in competition). It is not a direct quantitative removal or capacity measure, so classifying it as 'other' is appropriate and consistent with the source description (S07-E02, S07-E05).

S07-E02 and S07-E05 describe a clear competitive hierarchy where short-chain PFAS (PFBA, PFBS) have larger reductions in removal efficiency when in binary solutions with their longer-chain homologues (PFOA, PFOS), and that PFOS significantly reduced PFBA and PFBS removal while competition between PFOA and PFOS was relatively minor. This supports the detailed interpretation of competitive hierarchy and behavior in the record.

This endpoint synthesizes mechanistic explanation (electrostatic vs hydrophobic interactions) rather than a direct quantitative performance metric. Labeling it as 'other' matches its mechanistic nature and is consistent with the source (S07-E02, S07-E05).

S07-E02 notes that hydrophobic interaction mainly drives long-chain PFAS adsorption while short-chain PFAS uptake relies more on electrostatic interactions and micropore accessibility. S07-E05 adds that electrostatic interactions (short-chain) are more vulnerable to competitive displacement than hydrophobic interactions (long-chain). These statements directly support the interpretation about mechanisms underpinning the competitive hierarchy.

The source describes bisolute (binary) PFAS experiments conducted in controlled batch systems using prepared PFAS solutions (S07-E02, S07-E03), i.e., simplified systems rather than complex natural waters. From these design features, it follows that such tests may not fully represent competitive behavior in complex natural waters with multiple PFAS and co-constituents, justifying this as a design-inferred limitation.

The competitive adsorption section reports changes in removal efficiency (%) between single- and binary-solute systems and specific percentage reductions (S07-E02, S07-E05) but does not present absolute removal efficiencies or sorbed amounts for each PFAS in the binary systems in the cited text. This justifies, as a design-inferred comment, that only relative efficiency changes are available in the excerpt, limiting capacity-based comparisons.

The methods describe single-solute experiments with an initial PFAS concentration of 1.0 mg/L (S07-E03), but the provided competitive adsorption excerpt (S07-E02, S07-E05) does not explicitly state initial concentrations for the binary systems. This absence in the excerpt supports the limitation statement as design-inferred regarding uncertainty about degrees of competition.

S07-E03 states that for each experiment, single-solute PFAS solutions were prepared with an initial PFAS concentration of 1.0 mg L−1. The field explicitly identifies this as the single-solute reference concentration used for calculating changes in removal efficiency, which matches the cited value 1.0.
The source reports the initial PFAS concentration as 1.0 mg L−1 (S07-E03), which corresponds to the unit 'mg/L' used in the record.
S07-E03 and S07-E04 describe batch adsorption tests of 1 h duration. The value 1 (for contact time) agrees with this 1-hour test duration.
The contact time is described as 1 h (S07-E03, S07-E04). Using 'h' as the time unit is correct.

S07-E03 and S07-E04 state that 150 mL of PFAS solution was added to each 250 mL flask. The value 150 is therefore correct for solution volume per batch experiment; applying that batch configuration to the competitive tests is a reasonable design inference and is clearly noted in the qualifier.
The volume is reported as 150 mL in the source (S07-E03, S07-E04), so the unit 'mL' is appropriate.
S07-E03 states that flasks were placed in a thermostatically controlled shaker at 250 rpm. The value 250 matches this shaking speed.
The shaker speed is given as 250 rpm (S07-E03), so the unit 'rpm' is correct.

S07-E02 describes 'Bisolute experiments' and 'binary-solute systems for various PFAS pairs,' indicating the presence of PFAS background mixtures in binary solutions. The value 'binary PFAS solute systems' faithfully captures this background mixture description.
This condition describes the qualitative nature of the background PFAS mixture rather than a numeric quantity, so an empty unit is appropriate and consistent with the source.
S07-E02 and S07-E05 state that the highest reduction in removal efficiency was recorded for PFBA when copresent with PFOA at −56%. The recorded value of -56 matches the reported percentage reduction.
The reduction in removal efficiency is explicitly expressed as a percentage in the source (−56%; S07-E02, S07-E05), so the unit '%' is correct.
S07-E05 reports that PFBA removal efficiency reduction when copresent with PFOS is −13.7%. The value -13.7 in the record is an exact match.
The change in removal efficiency is given in percent (−13.7%; S07-E05), supporting the '%' unit.
S07-E05 states that PFBA experiences a −9.7% reduction in removal efficiency when copresent with PFBS. The record’s value -9.7 matches this figure.
The reduction in removal efficiency for PFBA with PFBS is given as a percentage (−9.7%; S07-E05), so '%' is the correct unit.
S07-E05 reports that PFOS significantly reduced the removal efficiency of PFBS by −30.2%. The recorded value -30.2 matches this number exactly.
The PFBS removal efficiency change is expressed as −30.2% in the source (S07-E05), hence '%' is the appropriate unit.

Within the study, Figure 5c reports changes in removal efficiency (%) between single- and binary-solute systems for different PFAS pairs under a common batch setup using CAC BM (S07-E02, S07-E03, S07-E05). This common basis (same adsorbent, bench-scale batch conditions, same reference single-solute concentration) supports treating these relative changes as directly comparable with noted conditions, matching the 'comparable_with_conditions' status.

The reason explains that the reported metrics are percentage changes in removal efficiency relative to single-solute tests conducted under the same general bench-scale conditions and cautions against direct comparison with absolute removals from other systems. This is consistent with the description of Figure 5c (relative changes between single and binary systems; S07-E02, S07-E05) and the methods for single-solute tests (S07-E03).

Any interpretive or design-inferred fields are reasonable and clearly grounded in the reported experimental design, so the record is suitable for synthesis use.
